title: What is known about 1RB---_1LC0RF_0RA0LD_1LE1LA_1RF0LF_0LC0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB---_1LC0RF_0RA0LD_1LE1LA_1RF0LF_0LC0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state machine halts from blank tape. It belongs to a family of six holdouts with almost the same table (a relabelled relative (its F plays E's part)). Their tapes are made of the words 10 and 110, grouped in sections split by 000, and they grow slowly to the left. This page lists what has been established, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The engine is decoded and proved in Lean for every size: from one event to the next, a base-3 counter N gets 1, a binary counter M gets 1, and when M wraps a binary counter R gets 3. No event can halt; a halt can only come from what was called an overflow of R. That is now located exactly: everything from R on is one endless stream of two tokens with a recursive visit law (Lean, every size), and the event rule stops when a visit of it comes out in state C instead of E. What the machine does after such a visit is proved row by row but not yet composed into a law.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (A1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 186 cells have been visited and 74 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Sweep rules
claims.text: The head crosses runs of the words 01, 10, 011 or 110 in one state, rewriting each copy the same way, for any number of copies and any surrounding tape.

claims.title: No halt in 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator runs 3·10<sup>9</sup> steps without a halt.

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: A closed tape language with windows of 6 cells (closed, found and checked by bbtools.ctl, not yet in Lean) allows a halt only with A reading a 1 and 110001 from the head on: the first 1 of a word 110 followed by a section break 000 1.

claims.title: The first section
claims.text: At its visits to the left end (in state F) the tape starts F>0 0 1 0 (1 1 0)^k …; the record values of k: 10 at step 6,019,226, 11 at step 37,281,281, 12 at step 467,158,233, 13 at step 910,412,010, 14 at step 1,269,148,937, 15 at step 2,345,360,050. Its left-end configurations coincide with those of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RE_1LE--- at 47 of its first 50 visits (in the same order; that machine takes about 1.12 times more steps): the two machines do the same thing.

claims.title: Growth
claims.text: Each new 110 at the front costs about 2 to 3 times the steps of the previous one, the signature of a counter; the rest of the tape changes everywhere between visits, so the counter's digits are not simply blocks.

claims.title: The event rule, for every size
claims.text: From an event 0^∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [M] 1 [R] (N base 3 in 3-cell digits 100/110/010, M and R binary in 4-cell digits 0010/1010 and 1000/1010, low digit first) the machine reaches the next event with N + 1, M + 1 and, when M wraps, R + 3; 54 theorems, one per case (54 cases, exhaustive by construction of events.py, not by a Lean theorem; carries over k twos in N, i ones in M, j ones in R; the wrap of N at the left end), each with its exact step count and any tape beyond.

claims.title: The run follows the rule
claims.text: The run reaches the clean shape (R followed by 1 0 1 and blank tape) at step 118,003 (N = 35 (5 digits), M = 2 (2 digits), R = 0 (12 digits)); 5,556 (to step 3·106) consecutive events then follow the rule, until R = 4,095 = 212 − 1 at step 3·106, about to overflow. Counting all events of the form N, 0 [M] 1, anything: 47,902 of the first 3·106 steps follow from the previous one by the rule, 3,503 do not (wraps of M that reach the undecoded part).

claims.title: Token rows of the visit law
claims.text: Vis q x r x': the head enters the stream x from the left in state q and first leaves it to the left in state r, leaving x'. With tokens of two cells right of the event cell, 30 rows occur in 3·107 steps; each is a Lean theorem, conditional on the nested visits of the rest of the stream and valid for every stream.

claims.title: The a/z stream and M as a recursive visit law
claims.text: Everything from R on, blank tape included, is one stream of a = 10 and z = 00. A visit in state B turns the first z into a and every second a before it into z; it comes out in E when the first z is at an odd place (the binary increment of R, for every size: vb_odd, ve_odd) and in C when it is at an even place (vb_even). M + 1 without a wrap (m_inc) and with a wrap, where the stream gets three visits (m_wrap), for every size.

claims.title: The overflow of R is the even case of the stream law
claims.text: R has no end: when all its digits up to the blank tape are 1, the first z is at an even place and the visit comes out in C, leaving the digits shifted by one token. In the run of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- this first happens at step 20,645 (stream a18 then blank, left as (z a)9 a). That the event rule fails only there is read off the rules, not a Lean theorem.

claims.title: After a visit that comes out in C
claims.text: What the layer of c tokens (M) becomes after a visit of the a/z stream that comes out in C is given row by row in Visit.lean but not composed into a law; the left side is not yet in this form. The machine can halt only there (follows from the event rules, not itself a theorem).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. Its engine is now decoded and proved: a base-3 counter on the left and two binary counters on the right tick together, N and M by one per event and R by three each time M wraps. Only the overflows of R, where the machine reaches its rare transitions, remain a mystery.

facts.text: The event rule (N+1, M+1, R+3 on a wrap) for every size, in Lean.
Events by the rule in 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps.
The only place a halt could come from.

sections.heading: Three counters on one tape
html: At the moments we call events (the head in state A, on a 0, just right of the left counter) the tape reads
0∞ 1 0 [N] A> 0 [M] 1 [R] …

• N, a base-3 counter: 3-cell digits 100 = 0, 110 = 1, 010 = 2, most significant first, its lowest digit next to the head;
  • M, a binary counter: 4-cell digits 0010 = 0, 1010 = 1, lowest digit first (next to the head);
  • R, a second binary counter after a single 1: 4-cell digits 1000 = 0, 1010 = 1, lowest digit first.
In the words a = 10, b = 110 of the older description, M's digits read as sections a| and aa, which is why the tape looked like sections of a's split by 000.

sections.heading: One event: N + 1, M + 1, and R + 3 when M wraps
html: From one event to the next the head runs right over M (and over R only when M wraps), comes back, crawls into N, adds one there and returns. The net effect:

counterchange per event
N+1 in base 3; trailing 2s carry; when N = 2…2 it becomes 0…0 with one digit more (the tape grows 3 cells at the left)
M+1 in binary; trailing 1s carry; from 1…1 it wraps to 0…0 (same width)
Runchanged, except when M wraps: then +3 in binary

So N counts events (mod 3width), M counts them mod 2width, and R gains 3 every 2width of M events: two different bases running side by side. Example from the run of 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- (M with 2 digits, R with 8): at steps 12,203, 12,223, 12,243, 12,253, 12,345 the triple (N, M, R) is (5, 0, 92), (6, 1, 92), (7, 2, 92), (8, 3, 92), (9, 0, 95).

Each case of this rule is a theorem in lean/Events.lean, proved for every size: 9 cases for N (lowest digit 0 or 1 after 0, 1 or k+2 twos, or the wrap of 2…2 at the left end), times 6 for M and R (no wrap, carry over i+1 ones, or a wrap of M with i+1 digits combined with the 4 cases of R's two low bits and a carry over j ones). 54 cases (exhaustive by construction of events.py), one theorem each, with its exact step count, e.g. 12i + 12j + 10k + 116 steps for a carry over k twos in N, a wrap of M with i+1 digits and R ending in 10 followed by j ones. When M does not wrap, nothing right of M is read, so these rules hold whatever lies beyond.

sections.heading: How long the run keeps this shape
html: In the clean shape R is followed by 1 0 1 and blank tape. This run reaches it at step 118,003 (N = 35 (5 digits), M = 2 (2 digits), R = 0 (12 digits)) and then 5,556 (to step 3·106) consecutive events follow the rule, until R = 4,095 = 212 − 1 at step 3·106, about to overflow.

An overflow of R (its carry running into the cells after it) is not covered by the rules: there the head goes past R and rebuilds the right part; in 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- the transition D1 (the only way into F, whose 1 halts) is used in the first 105 steps only at steps 138, 1,008, 3,177, 7,571 (before the clean shape) and 20,756, 53,353, 92,444, 92,861 (at the first three overflows of R). After the first overflows the cells right of R are no longer just 1 0 1: they hold a further structure starting 1 0 1 1 0 …, and M and R take other widths. Counting every event whose left part is N and whose right part starts 0 [M] 1, 47,902 events in the first 3·106 steps follow from the previous one by the rule and 3,503 do not (the wraps of M that touch the undecoded part); at step 3·106: N = 4,830 (10 digits), M with 1 digit, R with 5 digits.

sections.heading: Two words and a separator
html: Write a for 1 0 and b for 1 1 0. Apart from a few cells at the ends, the tape is a string of a's and b's broken into sections by extra 0s (0 0 0 between two 1s). At its visits to the left end the first section is a b b … b followed by a's and b's, and the later sections are mostly runs of a's. Writing 1 for a and 2 for b, the tape at step 645,244,842 of the first sibling is 1222222222222222 | 111 | 111 | 11111 | 111 | 12 | 11111112 | 111111111 | 11111 | 11111 | 1 | 111 | 1 | 11.

sections.heading: Sweeps and an inner counter
html: The head moves through runs of words in one state, rewriting each copy the same way, for example A turning 0 1 1 into 1 0 0 or B turning 1 0 into 0 1 (proved in Lean for any number of copies: a_right_01, a_right_011, b_right_10, b_right_110, f_right_10). Its excursions do not usually reach the ends: the turning points far from the left end follow the ruler pattern of a binary counter with digits four cells wide (in a stretch of 17,000 steps from step 28,601 of the first sibling the far turning points are 43, 47, 43, 51, 43, 47, 43, 55, … cells from the left end). The ends are visited rarely, and each visit to the left end finds the whole tape rearranged.

Each new b costs about 2 to 3 times as many steps as the one before, as a counter would.

sections.heading: Six siblings
html: Five of the six differ only in E1 and F0 (F1 halts in all of them); F is entered only from D reading 1, so F0 runs every time D finds a 1, and the five really are different machines. The sixth is a relabelled relative. All six show the same tape language and the same slow front.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The machine halts only when A reads a 1. A closed tape language with windows of six cells (an over-approximation of every configuration reachable from blank tape, found and checked by bbtools.ctl) allows that only with 110001 from the head on: A on the first 1 of a word 1 1 0 that ends a section. Whether the run ever puts A there is the open question.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.065). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.054).
After 109 steps the tape spans 186 cells (145 left of the start, 35 right), with a density of 1s of 0.398.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: What is left
html: The engine is proved; the halting question now sits entirely in the overflows. No event can halt, since every rule is a run of the machine; a halt can only come between events that the rules do not cover. Open: (1) the overflow of R as a rule: what N, M, R and the cells after R become; (2) the layered layout that follows (the part right of R starting 1 0 1 1 0), which seems to hold further counters; (3) whether the iterated overflows ever produce the halting pattern. The left counter N alone never causes trouble: its wrap at the left end is one of the proved cases.

sections.heading: One visit of a stream
html: Cut the tape right of the event cell into tokens of two cells: z = 00, a = 10, c = 01. Everything from R on, the blank tape included, is one stream of a and z, and one visit of the head in state B does this to it: the first z becomes a, and every second a before it becomes z.

If the first z is at an odd place the visit comes out in state E: with digits a z = 0 and a a = 1 this is the binary increment of R. If it is at an even place (all digits 1 up to the blank tape) the visit comes out in state C and leaves the digits shifted by one token. So R has no overflow into something else; the rare case is a visit that comes out in C.

Both cases, and M's increment and wrap (three visits of the stream), are proved in Lean for every size from 30 token rows, each of which is a small theorem about one token and the nested visits of the rest. What the c tokens of M do after a visit that comes out in C is in those rows but not yet composed; that is where the question of halting now sits.

summary: Two-word sweeper: a base-3 counter N and binary counters M and R; each event adds 1 to N and to M and, when M wraps, 3 to R (proved in Lean for every size); the overflows of R and the layered layout after them are not decoded.
